content.title: About
content.content: Cake and cupcake are baked goods made from a batter enriched with eggs, sugar, butter and milk. A cake is usually larger, multi‑layered and decorated with frosting, fruit or chocolate, while a cupcake is a single‑serve portion, often flavored with dried fruit, nuts or spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cakes originated in ancient Rome where they were called "placenta" and sweetened with honey and cheese.
Modern cupcakes appeared in 19th‑century England as "tea cakes" served with afternoon tea.
The world’s largest cake, baked in 2012 in the USA, weighed over 6 tons.
The classic American Red Velvet cake gets its vivid color from food coloring, not beet juice.
In Japan, “mochi cupcakes” replace wheat flour with glutinous rice flour for a chewy texture.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Cakes and cupcakes provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and dairy in the batter deliver B12, niacin and riboflavin, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Milk products contribute to bone and tooth strength.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit and berries
items.content: Cakes topped with fresh fruit or berries add vitamin C and polyphenols.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour, nuts or dried fruit raises fiber content, supporting digestion.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large portions can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Butter‑based cakes contain saturated fats that may affect cholesterol when consumed excessively.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Eggs, milk, nuts and wheat are common allergens that can trigger reactions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional wheat flour contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cake is typically served in slices, often accompanied by tea or coffee. Cupcakes are convenient as a snack and can be taken on the go. Both can be further decorated with frosting, sprinkles or fresh berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store finished cake in the refrigerator, covered with plastic wrap, for up to 3‑5 days. Cupcakes keep best in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days, or refrigerated for longer storage.

egg-sandwich-on-wheat-bread-with-meat-an.title: Egg sandwich with meat and cheese on wheat bread

content.title: About
content.content: The sandwich consists of two slices of wheat bread filled with a boiled egg, a slice of cooked or fried meat (such as ham or turkey) and melted cheese. It is a balanced snack providing protein, carbohydrates and fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bread supplies slowly digestible carbs that help maintain energy levels.
Eggs are one of the most nutrient‑dense foods, containing all essential amino acids.
The combination of meat and cheese makes this sandwich popular in school cafeterias and fast‑food outlets.
A traditional English "Full English" often includes a similar egg‑and‑bacon sandwich.
Preparation takes only a few minutes, making it ideal for an on‑the‑go breakfast.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Egg, meat and cheese together provide about 20‑25 g of protein, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat contain vitamins B2, B6 and B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, which contributes to bone and tooth health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Wheat bread, especially whole‑grain, adds dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Energy balance
items.content: The mix of carbs, protein and fat provides lasting satiety and stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, cheese or other dairy components.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed meats and cheese often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should choose lean meat and low‑salt cheese.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Cheese and fatty meat can increase saturated fat intake, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which is unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed hot, lightly toasted on a pan or toaster, or cold as a quick snack. Add fresh vegetables (tomatoes, lettuce) to boost vitamins and fiber.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store bread in a dry place, and keep meat and cheese refrigerated. For longer storage, separate the ingredients.

content.title: About
content.content: A fish sandwich is a fast‑food item consisting of a breaded and fried fish fillet placed between two buns and topped with melted cheese. It is often served with sauce, lettuce, and fries. The cheese adds a creamy note and makes the sandwich more filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first fish sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 1920s as an alternative to chicken and beef fast food.
White fish such as cod or pollock is commonly used because it pans easily and cooks quickly.
Cheese‑topped versions became popular in the 1970s when processed American cheese was added for a smoother texture.
In some countries the sandwich is served on flatbreads or baguettes, adapting the concept to local tastes.
The breading often includes spices like paprika and garlic, giving the fish a flavorful crust.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Fish provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish is rich in B12 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Fried fish in a light batter is quickly digested, making the sandwich a convenient quick meal.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Frying and cheese increase calories and saturated fat levels.

items.title: Allergy to fish or dairy
items.content: People with food allergies may react to the fish or cheese.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Sauces and cheese often contain a lot of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Trans fats in breading
items.content: If the breading is fried in reused oil, trans fats may form, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is usually served hot, split in half. It can be topped with lettuce, pickles, tomato, and tartar sauce. For a lighter option, baked fish can replace the fried fillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in foil or plastic. Keep the breading and fish separate to prevent the buns from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Tempura is a Japanese dish where pieces of fish, tofu and assorted vegetables are coated in a light batter and quickly deep‑fried. The cooking method preserves the natural flavors of the ingredients while the crisp crust adds a pleasant texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tempura was introduced to Japan in the 16th century by Portuguese missionaries.
The traditional batter is made from cold water and flour without leavening agents, resulting in a delicate, airy coating.
Common fish used include white fish such as snapper or salmon, which pair well with tofu that absorbs the batter’s flavor.
Vegetables are usually sliced thinly or cut into bite‑size pieces to ensure rapid cooking.
Tempura is often served with a dipping sauce made from dashi, mirin and soy sauce, sometimes enhanced with grated daikon.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish and tofu provide complete protein essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fatty fish such as salmon contain omega‑3s that support heart and brain health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables in tempura (e.g., carrots, bell peppers, broccoli) are rich in vitamins A, C and potassium.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Tempura contains no added sugars, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Brief frying retains most nutrients while the light crust is gentle on the digestive system.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Because it is deep‑fried, tempura can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to fish or shellfish should avoid this dish.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Dipping sauces are often salty; moderation is advised.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Overheating oil (above 180 °C) can produce acrylamides; keep frying temperature around 170‑180 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tempura hot, dipping each piece in tempura sauce or soy sauce with grated ginger. A squeeze of lemon or a side of grated daikon adds freshness. It pairs well with steamed rice or a light salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Tempura is best enjoyed immediately. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, though the crust will lose its crunch. Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 5‑7 minutes to restore texture.

content.title: About
content.content: The canned orange juice pack (item 3934) is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from ripe oranges, pasteurised and sealed in a hermetic pouch. The juice retains a bright orange colour, a sweet‑tart flavour and the fresh aroma of oranges.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Orange juice is one of the most popular fruit drinks worldwide.
Pouch packaging preserves a higher proportion of vitamin C compared with long‑term bottle storage.
Pouches are lightweight and space‑efficient, simplifying transport and storage.
Orange juice contains natural flavonoids such as hesperidin, which have antioxidant properties.
In some markets the pouch is considered more eco‑friendly because the material is often recyclable.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Orange juice is an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and cell growth, especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in the juice protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Being mostly water, the juice contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The juice can contain a notable amount of natural sugars; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oranges.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain versions may include additives (e.g., potassium sorbate) to extend shelf life.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The juice is ready to drink straight from the pouch. It can be enjoyed chilled, used in cocktails, smoothies, culinary recipes, or as a base for marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened pouches in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Prune juice is a 100% natural beverage made from ripe dried plums (prunes). It has a rich sweet‑tart flavor, deep burgundy color, and a distinctive aroma. The juice contains no added sugar, preservatives, or artificial colors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Prunes have been used in cooking and traditional medicine for millennia.
Prune juice is often employed as a natural sweetener in baked goods and sauces.
Ancient cultures regarded prunes as a food that supports digestive health.
The juice retains most of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh plums thanks to minimal processing.
Prunes belong to the Rosaceae family and are closely related to plums, cherries, and apricots.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: The juice provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, which supports regular bowel movements and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a role in blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain electrolyte balance, normal blood pressure, and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds and vitamin C in the juice combat free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Prune juice is traditionally used to relieve constipation due to its natural laxative effect.

items.title: High natural sugar content
items.content: Even without added sugar, the juice contains natural sugars, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of the juice may irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Plum allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to plum components can occur.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Prune juice is relatively calorie‑dense; excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prune juice can be enjoyed on its own, added to smoothies, cocktails, sauces, and marinades. It is often used in diet plans to improve bowel regularity. Diluting with water is recommended if the flavor is too intense.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator after opening, in a tightly sealed bottle, for up to 7‑10 days. Unopened packages should be kept in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberries are bright red, juicy, fragrant fruits of the plant Fragaria × ananassa, a member of the rose family. The modern garden strawberry is a hybrid that originated in Europe in the 18th century from species of North and South American origin. They have a sweet, slightly tart flavor and are eaten fresh or used in jams, desserts, drinks, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, a strawberry is not a true berry but an aggregate accessory fruit.
The small "seeds" on the outside are actually separate fruits called achenes, and a strawberry can have around 200 of them.
Strawberries belong to the rose family, as do apples and peaches.
The modern garden strawberry is a hybrid of two wild species from the Americas.
Strawberries are among the most popular berries in the world.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Strawberries are an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Anthocyanins and ellagic acid are plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides manganese and folate
items.content: These nutrients support normal metabolism and cell function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Strawberries contribute fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Relatively low in sugar
items.content: Compared with many fruits, strawberries are lower in sugar and calories.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Strawberries can cause allergic reactions in some people, including itching, hives, or swelling.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Conventionally grown strawberries may carry pesticide residues, so wash them thoroughly before eating.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts may cause bloating or stomach upset in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Salicylate sensitivity
items.content: Strawberries contain natural salicylates, which may cause reactions in people who are sensitive to them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Strawberries can be eaten fresh, sliced into salads, yogurt, oatmeal, and desserts, or blended into smoothies. They can also be made into jams, sauces, and baked goods. Wash them just before eating and remove the green leafy tops.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unwashed strawberries in the refrigerator in a single layer in a breathable container and use them within a few days. Remove any moldy berries right away so mold does not spread. Wash just before eating. For longer storage, strawberries can be washed, dried, hulled, and frozen.
